title: SCALING WRITES
subtitle: When writes outgrow one machine, absorb the spikes, write in batches, split the data, and write less.
footer: Theory: DDIA ch 3 Storage and retrieval · DDIA ch 6 Partitioning · DDIA ch 11 Stream processing

items: Sustained writes exceed what one primary handles (roughly 10k+ per second for simple rows).
Write traffic is spiky: events, clicks, telemetry.
Data is append-mostly and read in aggregate (counts, time series).
Every event is an individual synchronous DB write. Spikes overwhelm the database.
A queue/log (Kafka) absorbs spikes and decouples producers from the DB. Consumers write in batches.
Shard by a key that spreads load evenly (hash of id); each shard takes a fraction of the writes.
Reduce the writes: pre-aggregate (10k clicks → 1 row per minute), and use write-optimized LSM storage.
Can the client get a quick ack while the work happens later? Put a durable log (Kafka) in front.
Can writes be grouped? Batch inserts in consumers.
Can you store less? Pre-aggregate (one row per key per minute instead of one per event).
Still too much for one node? Shard by a key that spreads load evenly.
Write-heavy and simple key access? Use an LSM-based store such as Cassandra.

blocks.text: "Clicks arrive at 10k/s with spikes, so they go to Kafka first. A stream job aggregates per ad per minute, which cuts the database writes by orders of magnitude."

items: A hot partition: one key still lands on one shard.
Losing data by acknowledging before anything is durable.
Using a B-tree OLTP database for a firehose of append-only events.

blocks.text: Used in: Top-K videos (YouTube), Ad click aggregator, Web crawler, Metrics monitoring (Datadog), Fitness tracking (Strava), Post search (Facebook), Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel)
